lines.trans: Nastya, you will drive me crazy one of these days!
One must not run into the kitchen so unexpectedly.
Chef, I have a very urgent question.
What is the correct term for a female chef?
A female head chef is a freak of nature.
Why do you speak so unfairly?
Because a real kitchen is a man's business!
Then a freak of nature is sitting in our hall.
Where exactly is this woman sitting?
She is sitting in our main dining hall.
Where did this strange guest come from?
This is the head chef from the neighboring restaurant!
What do the rivals want in my restaurant?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to run in'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Нельзя так неожиданно вбегать на кухню.
examples.trans: One must not run into the kitchen so unexpectedly.

meanings.note: важный вопрос = an important matter
важный вопрос = an important matter

examples.text: Я тебе утром говорил: не торопись. Это очень важный вопрос.
examples.trans: I told you this morning: don't rush. It's a very important question.

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'where'.

examples.text: А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
examples.trans: Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'main' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('the main thing') (neuter главное, used as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The main thing is, don't worry.
The most important thing is the people.

говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to speak', forming an aspectual pair with 'сказать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to speak, to talk') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Declinable feminine noun meaning 'female guest', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Все внимание! Гостья пробует блюдо новичка.
examples.trans: Attention everyone! The guest is tasting the newcomer's dish.
The guest is tasting the newcomer's dish.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'matter', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('matter, business') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('case (in court)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'вести'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to drive to'.

examples.trans: Nastya, you will drive me crazy one of these days!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'woman' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Твоя жена очень мудрая женщина. Ты её слушай.
examples.trans: Your wife is a very wise woman. You listen to her.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'быть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to forget', paired with 'забывать'.

examples.trans: Don't forget to wash the toilet.

examples.text: Сейчас будешь чинить трубу. И унитаз не забудь помыть.
examples.trans: Now you're going to fix the pipe. And don't forget to wash the toilet.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'hall', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('living room') (regional/colloquial) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Understood. And who is managing the dining room?

meanings.note: + genitive: 'из мэрии' = from the town hall

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, я уже знаю. Мне звонили из мэрии.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, I already know. The town hall called me.

meanings.note: вот именно = that's just it, quite right
Secondary conversational sense ('namely') (а именно = namely) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Именно это я и хотел сказать.
examples.trans: That is justamente what I wanted to say.

examples.text: Вот именно. Но мне сдаваться нельзя.
examples.trans: Exactly. But I must not give up.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.
Secondary conversational sense ('as') (как вы знаете = as you know) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'someday'.
Secondary conversational sense ('ever (in questions)') (ты когда-нибудь был там?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Когда-нибудь ты захочешь помириться со своим папой.
examples.trans: Someday you will want to make up with your dad.

examples.text: Вы любили когда-нибудь? Смотрите, мэр стоит на коленях!
examples.trans: Have you ever loved? Look, the mayor is on his knees!

meanings.note: From German 'Konkurrent' / Latin 'concurrens' ('running together', rival).

examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Relational adjective formed with the Slavic suffix '-ский' ('pertaining to'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('men's, masculine').

examples.trans: These are our little men's secrets!

examples.text: Я всегда держу своё мужское слово.
examples.trans: I always keep my word as a man.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: of things, places, films: 'как называется ...?' = what is ... called?

examples.trans: The operation is called Golden Yard.

examples.text: Товарищ генерал, операция называется Золотой ярд.
examples.trans: Comrade General, the operation is called Golden Yard.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'стоящий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('real, genuine').
Secondary conversational sense ('present, current') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ваня, да пойми ты наконец! Это настоящий успех.
examples.trans: Vanya, understand at last! This is real success.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

нельзя.gloss: it is not allowed; one can't

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'it is not allowed'.
Secondary conversational sense ('impossible, can't') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Not allowed? All right, I'll go and do my homework.

meanings.note: это неожиданно = this is unexpected

examples.text: Это неожиданно, но ваш торт не такой плохой.
examples.trans: This is unexpected, but your cake isn't so bad.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'справедливо'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Why do you speak so unfairly?

examples.text: Ты поступила со мной очень несправедливо.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'куда').

examples.trans: Where does that word come from?
Thief, thief. Where does that word come from?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'mistake'.

examples.trans: This is some kind of mistake!
There are many serious mistakes in the case.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'that's why'.
Secondary conversational sense ('that's why') (потому и = that's exactly why) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я устал, потому что много работал.
examples.trans: I'm tired because I worked a lot.
I'm at home because I'm ill.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'right'.

examples.text: Это правильно. Я приглашаю вас в общественный совет.
examples.trans: That's right. I'm inviting you onto the public council.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to come', forming an aspectual pair with 'приходить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Security will be here any moment.

examples.text: Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
examples.trans: Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.

meanings.note: на природе = out in nature, outdoors

examples.text: Мы давно на природе не были!
examples.trans: We have not been out in nature for a long time!

examples.text: Вот так бы на природе, да? Мы давно на природе не были!
examples.trans: Now if we were out in nature, right? We have not been out in nature for a long time!

examples.text: Вот так бы на природе, да?
examples.trans: Now if we were out in nature, right?

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'идеть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to sit', forming an aspectual pair with 'посидеть'.

examples.trans: Why are you sitting in the corner?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'neighboring' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.text: В соседнем зале играет тихая музыка.
examples.trans: Quiet music plays in the neighboring hall.

examples.text: За соседним столиком сидели приятные люди.
examples.trans: Pleasant people were sitting at the next table.
To a guest at the next table.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'рочный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('urgent, pressing').

examples.trans: This is a very urgent matter.

examples.text: Яков Григорьевич, у меня срочный вопрос к вам.
examples.trans: Yakov Grigoryevich, I have an urgent question for you.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'транный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strange, odd').
Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Secondary conversational sense ('then, in that case') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'head chef', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Шеф-повар лично руководит работой на кухне.
examples.trans: The head chef personally oversees the work in the kitchen.
The head chef manages the entire kitchen.

examples.text: Они привели нового шеф-повара прямо из Индии.
examples.trans: They brought a new chef straight from India.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
